name: Gamma Regression
analogy: Think of it as a weather forecaster who predicts rainfall amounts: the forecast can never be negative, and a forecast of heavy rain comes with proportionally wide uncertainty while a forecast of drizzle is tight. Gamma regression forecasts always-positive sizes, such as a bar's range, in exactly that way.

steps.title: Take a target that is always positive and skewed
steps.description: The target is a size that must be above zero, with many modest values and an occasional very large one: the high-minus-low range of a bar, the time until an order fills, or the size of slippage. This lopsided shape is what the model is built for.
steps.inExample: The target is the high-minus-low range of the next 5-minute MNQ bar, in points, from 20,000 past bars.

steps.title: Combine the features into one score
steps.description: Each feature gets a weight, and the weighted features are added into a single score for the bar. The score is not the forecast yet; it lives on a logarithmic scale so that features act by multiplication rather than addition.
steps.inExample: A high volume and a large recent range push the score up, while a quiet time of day pulls it down.

steps.title: Turn the score into a positive expected size
steps.description: The score is exponentiated, which can only produce a positive number. A feature that adds a little to the score therefore multiplies the expected size by a fixed percentage. A weight reads naturally as: each extra unit of this feature raises the expected range by this many percent.
steps.inExample: The bar's score converts into an expected range of 26 points.

steps.title: Let the uncertainty grow with the size
steps.description: The model assumes the spread of outcomes is a fixed fraction of the expected size, so a prediction of a large range carries a proportionally larger margin than a small one. That fixed fraction is estimated separately after the weights are found.
steps.inExample: The spread comes out at about 45 percent of the expected range, so a 26 point expectation has a typical miss of about 12 points.

steps.title: Fit the weights by repeated reweighted fitting
steps.description: The weights are found by a routine that fits a weighted straight-line problem over and over, reweighting each round according to the current fit, until the numbers settle. It usually settles in a handful of rounds and judges misses by their ratio to the expected size, not their raw difference.
steps.inExample: The routine settles after 6 rounds on weights that make the training bars' ranges as likely as possible.

steps.title: Read off the expected size and its range
steps.description: For a new bar the model returns the expected size and, using the estimated spread, a range of likely values that is skewed upward, with more room above the center than below.
steps.inExample: For the next bar the model returns 26 points, with 80 percent of outcomes between about 13 and 42 points.

useFor.task: Forecasting the range of the next bar
useFor.example: Predicting the next 5-minute MNQ bar's high-minus-low range to set a stop distance that is neither too tight nor wasteful.

useFor.task: Forecasting time until a limit order fills
useFor.example: Predicting how many seconds a resting limit order near the touch will wait, from the spread and recent volatility.
Predicting the average slippage in points on a market order of 5 contracts so costs can be built into position sizing.

useFor.task: Predicting a volatility level for risk
useFor.example: Forecasting the average true range over the next hour as an input to a separate risk-limit layer.

avoidWhen: The target is sometimes exactly zero, such as slippage on well-filled orders; the model cannot produce a zero, and a model that allows exact zeros, such as Tweedie regression, fits better.
The relationship between features and the size is strongly nonlinear; gradient boosting under the same positive-size scoring handles interactions that a weighted sum cannot.

example.scenario: At 11:05 New York time a trader wants to place a stop for a trade on MNQ and asks how big the next 5-minute bar's range is likely to be, using a model trained on 20,000 past bars.

input.summary: The features of the bar that just closed.

fields.name: average true range, 14 bars
fields.meaning: The typical high-to-low travel of a recent bar.

fields.name: range of the last bar
fields.meaning: The high minus the low of the bar that just closed.

fields.name: volume against its 20-bar average
fields.meaning: How heavy trading was compared with the recent norm.

fields.name: minutes since the 09:30 open
fields.meaning: How far into the session the bar is, since ranges shrink toward midday.

fields.name: bid-ask spread
fields.value: one tick, a quarter of a point
fields.meaning: The gap between the best buy and sell prices.

output.summary: An expected range and a skewed range of likely values.

fields.name: expected range of the next bar
fields.meaning: The model's average expectation for the next bar's high minus low.

fields.name: typical spread around it
fields.meaning: About 45 percent of the expected size, which is how the model ties spread to size.

fields.name: 80 percent range
fields.meaning: Skewed upward: far more room above the center than below.

example.reading: A stop closer than about 13 points will often be hit by ordinary bar movement, and a stop beyond about 42 points is rarely needed to survive one bar. Compare the prediction with the realized ranges on later bars: the share of bars inside the 80 percent range should be near 80 percent.
